theme: The law’s limits; the wretched man’s cry
readingInstruction: Read Romans 7:1-25. This is one of the most debated chapters in the Bible. Read verses 1-6 on being released from the law, verses 7-13 on the law and sin, and verses 14-25 on the struggle. Notice the cry in verse 24 and the answer in verse 25.
settingTheScene: Paul has said that believers are not under law but under grace (6:14). A listener might ask, “Is the law then sin?” Chapter 7 answers. The law is holy, righteous, and good, but it cannot save or sanctify, because it meets a heart already enslaved to sin. The chapter ends with the cry of a man who sees the war within himself. Christians have argued for centuries about who this “I” is.
observation: “Likewise, my brothers, you also have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who has been raised from the dead, in order that we may bear fruit for God” (7:4).
“What shall we say then? That the law is sin? By no means! Yet if it had not been for the law, I would not have known sin” (7:7).
“So then, the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good” (7:12).
“For I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate” (7:15).
“For I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh” (7:18).
“For I delight in the law of God, in my inner being” (7:22).
“Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (7:24).
“Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!” (7:25).
interpretation:
Paul opens with an illustration from marriage. A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives; if he dies, she is free to marry another. In the same way, believers have “died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who has been raised from the dead.” The goal is fruit for God. Before, “our sinful passions, aroused by the law, were at work in our members to bear fruit for death.” Now we serve “in the new way of the Spirit and not in the old way of the written code.” This is the contrast between the old covenant and the new, a key idea in the progressive covenantal reading: the Mosaic covenant has served its purpose and been fulfilled in Christ.

Is the law then to blame? “By no means!” The law shows what sin is. Paul uses the tenth commandment, “You shall not covet,” as an example. Sin took the opportunity in the commandment to produce all kinds of covetousness. “So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good.” The problem is not the law but sin, which uses the good law to show its evil.

Then, from verse 14, Paul shifts into the present tense and speaks of a deep inner conflict. “I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate.” “I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out.” “I delight in the law of God, in my inner being, but I see in my members another law waging war against the law of my mind.” He cries: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” And the answer: “Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!”

Who is this speaker? Faithful interpreters differ. Some (Augustine in his later writings, Luther, Calvin, and many Reformed writers) see the regenerate Christian, because the speaker delights in God’s law and hates sin, which an unbeliever would not. Others (Origen, and many modern scholars) see Paul describing the person under the law before Christ, or Israel under Sinai, speaking in the first person for dramatic effect. Both agree on the main point: the law cannot rescue, and only Christ can. Both also agree that the believer’s experience includes a real struggle with remaining sin (Galatians 5:17). The cry of verse 24 is not the last word. Chapter 8 begins, “There is therefore now no condemnation.”

If you have felt this conflict, you are not strange. It is evidence that something has changed, that you want what is good. The answer is not to try harder but to look to the deliverer.
connection: Exodus 20:17 is the tenth commandment. Jeremiah 31:31-34 and Ezekiel 36:26-27 promise the new covenant. Galatians 5:16-24 describes the war between flesh and Spirit. Galatians 3:19-25 explains the purpose of the law as a guardian until Christ. 2 Corinthians 3:4-18 contrasts the old and new covenants. Hebrews 8:6-13 says the new covenant is better. Psalm 119 shows delight in the law. 1 John 1:8-2:2 deals with remaining sin and our advocate.
application:
Name an area where you do what you do not want. Bring it to Christ, not just to your willpower.

Say verse 25 aloud as an answer to your own wretchedness.

Thank God that the law is holy, and that Christ has done what the law could not.
prayerPrompts: Confess where you do what you hate and fail to do what you want.
Cry, “Wretched man that I am,” and thank him for Jesus.
Thank him that there is now no condemnation.
